lessons.title: Binary Tree Structure And Terminology
lessons.objective: Define every binary tree term precisely, implement a TreeNode class, and understand the structural properties that determine algorithm choice.
concepts: TreeNode: val, left, right pointers
Root: the single entry point with no parent
Leaf: a node with no children (left=null, right=null)
Height: longest path from a node down to any leaf
Depth: distance from the root down to a node
Subtree: a node and all its descendants
Full binary tree: every node has 0 or 2 children
Complete binary tree: all levels filled except possibly the last, filled left to right
Perfect binary tree: all leaves at the same level, all internal nodes have 2 children
Balanced binary tree: for every node, left and right subtree heights differ by at most 1
lessons.explanation: A binary tree is a hierarchical data structure where each node has at most two children, called left and right. The root is the topmost node with no parent. A leaf is a node with both left and right as null. Height of a node is the length of the longest path from that node down to any leaf. Height of a leaf is 0. Height of an empty tree is -1 by convention. Depth of a node is its distance from the root. The root has depth 0. These two are commonly confused: height measures downward from a node, depth measures upward from the root. A full binary tree has every node with exactly 0 or 2 children. A complete binary tree has all levels fully filled except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right — this is the structure used by binary heaps. A perfect binary tree is full AND all leaves are at the same level. A balanced binary tree guarantees that for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most 1 — this balance condition is what makes AVL trees and red-black trees maintain O(log n) operations.
lessons.analogy: A binary tree is a family genealogy tree. The root is the oldest ancestor. Leaves are the youngest generation with no children. Height is how many generations descend from a person. Depth is how many generations back to the founder. A balanced tree is a family where every branch of the family has roughly the same number of generations — no one branch vastly longer than another. An unbalanced tree is a family where one branch has 10 generations and another has 2.

code_example.explanation: Height returns -1 for null (empty tree) so that leaf nodes correctly compute height = 1 + max(-1, -1) = 0. This convention is important: if you use 0 for null, leaf heights would be 1 and all height calculations would be off by one. Always establish height(null) = -1 before implementing any height-based algorithm.

common_mistakes: Confusing height and depth — height measures downward from a given node to the deepest leaf; depth measures upward from that node to the root; they are inverses; a node at depth 3 may have height 5 if it has a long subtree below it
Using height(null) = 0 instead of -1 — if null returns 0, a leaf node returns height 1 instead of 0, and all height-based balanced tree checks will be wrong by one

Thinking a balanced tree means all leaves are at the same depth — that is a perfect tree; a balanced tree only requires that for every node, the height difference between left and right subtrees is at most 1; leaves can be at different depths
lessons.interview_relevance: Interviewers start every tree problem with 'draw the tree and label the root, leaves, height, and depth' as a mental check. Confusing height and depth or full/complete/perfect in an explanation immediately signals unfamiliarity with tree fundamentals. Every subsequent tree lesson builds on these definitions.

flashcards.front: What is a Full Binary Tree?

theory_mcq.question: What distinguishes a LEAF node from any other node in a binary tree, and how does the lesson's `isLeaf` function verify this?

A leaf node has NO children — both its `left` and `right` pointers are null; `isLeaf` checks `node.left === null && node.right === null` (plus that the node itself isn't null), confirming no children exist
A leaf is any node whose depth equals the tree's height

theory_mcq.question: What is the key difference between HEIGHT and DEPTH, and why does the lesson define height of null as -1?
options: Height and depth are identical; both measure distance from the root

Height measures the longest path FROM a node DOWN to any leaf (a node-centric downward measure), while depth measures the distance FROM the root DOWN to a specific node (a root-centric measure); height of null is defined as -1 so that a leaf's height correctly evaluates to 1 + max(-1,-1) = 0 — giving leaf nodes height 0, single-child nodes height 1, and so on
Height is measured in edges; depth is measured in nodes
Height is only defined for the root; depth applies to all nodes
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson's definitions: 'Height: longest path from a node down to any leaf' vs 'Depth: distance from the root down to a node' — the null-height-as-(-1) convention is a deliberate design choice: since `1 + max(height(null), height(null)) = 1 + max(-1,-1) = 0`, leaf nodes correctly get height 0, making the recurrence consistent.

theory_mcq.question: What structural property makes a tree a PERFECT binary tree, and how does it differ from a COMPLETE binary tree?
options: Perfect and complete binary trees are the same structure

A perfect binary tree has ALL leaves at the same level AND all internal nodes have exactly 2 children — it is completely full at every level; a complete binary tree only requires all levels to be fully filled EXCEPT possibly the last, which must be filled LEFT TO RIGHT (allowing a partial last row); every perfect binary tree is complete, but not vice versa
A perfect binary tree is one where all values are sorted
A complete binary tree requires all nodes to have 0 or 2 children
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact definitions: 'Perfect binary tree: all leaves at the same level, all internal nodes have 2 children' vs 'Complete binary tree: all levels filled except possibly the last, filled left to right' — the distinction matters because complete binary trees are the backing structure for binary heaps (Module 9), while perfect trees serve as useful analysis tools.

logic_mcq.question: Why does `countNodes` use the formula `1 + countNodes(left) + countNodes(right)` rather than just `countNodes(left) + countNodes(right)`?
options: The +1 is an error; just left+right is correct

The +1 counts the CURRENT node itself — the formula says: the count of this subtree equals 1 (this node) plus the count of its left subtree plus the count of its right subtree; without the +1, the root and every internal node would be omitted from the count
The +1 only applies to leaf nodes
countNodes is equivalent to height and the formula doesn't matter
logic_mcq.explanation: The +1 represents the current node itself: `countNodes(node) = 1 (this node) + countNodes(node.left) + countNodes(node.right)` — this is the standard structural recursion pattern for tree counting, where the base case `countNodes(null) = 0` anchors the recursion, and each non-null node contributes exactly 1 to the total.

syntax_mcq.question: In `class TreeNode { constructor(val, left = null, right = null) }`, why are `left` and `right` given default values of null?
options: Default null values prevent the node from having children

Default null values allow `new TreeNode(5)` to create a leaf node without explicitly passing null for both children — the defaults correctly represent 'no children', while still allowing `new TreeNode(4, leftChild, rightChild)` to set both children at construction time; this is the same default-parameter convenience pattern used for LinkedList's `ListNode` in Module 6
null defaults make the constructor private
JavaScript requires null as the default for all object parameters
syntax_mcq.explanation: Matching the same pattern from Module 6's ListNode: default `null` parameters allow minimal construction (`new TreeNode(val)` for leaves) while still supporting full construction (`new TreeNode(val, left, right)` for internal nodes) — the null defaults cleanly represent the 'no child' state without requiring the caller to explicitly pass null.

lessons.title: DFS — Preorder, Inorder, Postorder
lessons.objective: Implement all three DFS traversal orders both recursively and iteratively, understand what each order produces, and know which order to use for each problem type.
concepts: DFS: explore as deep as possible before backtracking
Preorder: root → left → right (process node before children)
Inorder: left → root → right (process node between children)
Postorder: left → right → root (process node after children)
Recursive DFS: implicit call stack
Iterative DFS: explicit stack
Inorder of BST produces sorted sequence
Postorder for bottom-up information: height, size, diameter
lessons.explanation: Depth-First Search explores a tree by going as deep as possible along one branch before backtracking to explore other branches. The three orders differ only in when the current node is processed relative to its children. Preorder (root, left, right): process the current node first, then recurse left, then recurse right. Use this to copy a tree, serialise a tree, or prefix-expression evaluation. Inorder (left, root, right): recurse left first, process the current node, then recurse right. For a BST, this visits nodes in sorted ascending order. Postorder (left, right, root): recurse both children first, then process the current node. Use this for bottom-up computations where a node needs information from its children before it can be processed: height, size, diameter, and any problem where the answer at a node depends on answers from its subtrees. The recursive implementations are trivially short. Iterative implementations use an explicit stack to simulate the call stack and are required when the interviewer says 'solve this without recursion' or when stack overflow is a concern for deep trees.
lessons.analogy: DFS traversal orders are like three ways to read a book of nested chapters. Preorder is reading the chapter title before reading its sub-chapters — top-down. Inorder is reading the left sub-chapters, then the chapter title, then the right sub-chapters — produces alphabetical order for BSTs. Postorder is reading all sub-chapters before the chapter title — bottom-up, like summarising sub-chapters before writing the main chapter summary.

code_example.explanation: Iterative inorder uses a curr pointer to go left as far as possible, pushing each node to the stack. When curr is null, we backtrack by popping the stack. The popped node is the next inorder node. We then move to its right subtree and repeat. This exactly simulates the recursive inorder call stack: pushing left-ward nodes is equivalent to the recursive calls going left, and popping is the return from recursion.

common_mistakes: Pushing left before right in iterative preorder — since the stack pops LIFO, you must push right first so that left is on top and processed first; pushing left first produces right-left order
Confusing which traversal order produces sorted output for a BST — ONLY inorder (left-root-right) produces sorted ascending order; preorder and postorder do not

Using postorder for problems that need top-down information flow — postorder propagates information bottom-up (children to parent); for problems needing parent-to-child information (path from root, depth), use preorder or BFS
lessons.interview_relevance: DFS traversal is the foundation of virtually every tree problem. Interviewers expect all three orders to be produced instantly, both recursively and iteratively. 'Implement inorder iteratively' is a classic follow-up question once the recursive solution is given. Knowing inorder produces sorted BST output is specifically tested in BST problems in Lessons 8 and 9.

theory_mcq.question: What is the fundamental difference between preorder, inorder, and postorder DFS, and what determines which to use for a given problem?
options: The three traversals visit the same nodes in the same order; only the output differs

The three traversals differ in WHEN the current node is 'processed' relative to its children: preorder processes root FIRST (root→left→right, useful for top-down problems like path recording); inorder processes root BETWEEN children (left→root→right, producing sorted output from a BST); postorder processes root LAST (left→right→root, useful for bottom-up aggregation like height/diameter where child results are needed before the parent)
Preorder is always O(n); inorder and postorder are O(n log n)
Only preorder works recursively; inorder and postorder require iterative implementations
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson's explicit mapping: 'Preorder: root→left→right (process node before children)', 'Inorder: left→root→right (process node between children)', 'Postorder: left→right→root (process node after children)' — the ORDER of processing determines what information is available when a node is handled, which dictates which traversal fits each problem class.

theory_mcq.question: Why does inorder traversal of a BST produce a SORTED (ascending) sequence?
options: BST inorder produces sorted output only when the tree is balanced

The BST invariant guarantees all left subtree values < current node < all right subtree values — inorder visits left subtree FIRST (all values smaller than current), then current node, then right subtree (all values larger) — this recursive application of the BST invariant at every node guarantees the final sequence is strictly ascending
Inorder produces sorted output for any binary tree, not just BSTs
Inorder only produces sorted output when the tree was built from a pre-sorted array
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit concept: 'Inorder of BST produces sorted sequence' — the BST invariant (left < parent < right) applied recursively means inorder's left-root-right visit order naturally produces ascending values: every left subtree contains only values smaller than the current node, which is smaller than everything in the right subtree.

logic_mcq.question: For the reference tree (4/2,7/1,3,6,9), trace all three traversals. What sequences do preorder, inorder, and postorder produce?
options: All three produce [1,2,3,4,6,7,9]

Preorder: [4,2,1,3,7,6,9] (root first, then left subtree, then right); Inorder: [1,2,3,4,6,7,9] (sorted ascending for this BST); Postorder: [1,3,2,6,9,7,4] (leaves first, root last) — all confirmed by direct execution
All three produce [4,2,7,1,3,6,9]
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution against the lesson's stated console.log outputs: preorder [4,2,1,3,7,6,9] (root-left-right), inorder [1,2,3,4,6,7,9] (sorted, confirming this is a BST), postorder [1,3,2,6,9,7,4] (children before parent — leaves first, root last).

logic_mcq.question: In `preorderIterative`, why is the RIGHT child pushed BEFORE the LEFT child, even though preorder processes left before right?
options: The order doesn't matter for an iterative implementation

Since a stack is LIFO, pushing right FIRST means left is on TOP and will be POPPED (processed) FIRST — to achieve left-before-right processing order using a stack, you must push in REVERSE order: push right, then push left, so left is popped next; pushing left first would cause right to be processed before left, producing incorrect root-right-left order
Pushing right first is a bug; left should always be pushed first
The right child is always larger in a BST, so it's pushed first for efficiency
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the standard iterative preorder trick: because the stack pops from the top (LIFO), to process left before right, you push right first (goes to bottom) and left second (sits on top and is popped first) — this achieves the correct root→left→right order iteratively.

logic_mcq.question: In `inorderIterative`, what is the role of the `curr` pointer, and why does the loop condition `while (curr || stack.length)` need BOTH conditions?
options: curr is redundant; the stack alone is sufficient to track state

`curr` tracks which node is currently being explored leftward (before pushing to stack); the two conditions handle different states: `curr` being non-null means 'we're still descending left', while `stack.length` being non-zero means 'there are unprocessed nodes to backtrack to' — either condition alone would terminate the loop prematurely: if only `curr`, the loop ends when curr becomes null (at the leftmost node) before stack is drained; if only `stack.length`, the first iteration pushes nothing since curr starts before any push
curr is the previous node; the stack tracks all nodes
Both conditions are always true simultaneously; only one is needed
logic_mcq.explanation: The two conditions together cover the complete state space: `curr != null` drives the leftward descent phase (pushing nodes onto the stack), while `stack.length > 0` drives the backtrack-and-process phase (popping, recording, then moving to right child) — the loop continues as long as EITHER state is active, correctly handling all nodes including the rightmost.

syntax_mcq.question: In `preorder(root, result = [])`, why is `result` passed as a parameter rather than created fresh inside the function body?
options: Creating result inside would cause a syntax error

Passing `result` as an accumulator parameter means recursive calls can SHARE the SAME array rather than creating and then merging separate arrays at each level — all recursive calls append directly to the one shared result array, avoiding the overhead of creating O(n) intermediate arrays and spreading/concatenating them; the default `= []` handles the initial call where the caller doesn't provide a result array
result must be a parameter to work recursively; local variables don't persist
This pattern only works for preorder, not inorder or postorder
syntax_mcq.explanation: The accumulator pattern (shared mutable array passed through all calls) is more memory-efficient than returning and concatenating separate arrays at each level — all recursive invocations append to the SAME array object, and the top-level call either passes its own array or uses the default empty array, making this a clean single-allocation approach.

lessons.objective: Implement BFS level-order traversal using a queue, collect results grouped by level, and apply BFS to problems requiring level-by-level processing.
concepts: BFS: process all nodes at depth d before any at depth d+1
Queue as the BFS data structure: FIFO ensures level-by-level
Level grouping: track current level size within BFS loop
Right side view: last node at each level
Zigzag level order: alternate direction by level
Minimum depth: BFS finds it in O(n) before DFS worst case
Why BFS for shortest path: first time a node is visited is the shortest path
BFS vs DFS: when to choose each for tree problems
lessons.explanation: Breadth-First Search visits nodes level by level, processing all nodes at depth d before any node at depth d+1. A queue enforces this FIFO order: enqueue the root, then loop: dequeue a node, process it, enqueue its children. Since children are enqueued after their parent and dequeued after all siblings, the level-by-level order is maintained automatically. Level grouping: at the start of each level, the queue contains exactly the nodes of that level. Record the queue size before processing, then dequeue exactly that many nodes and enqueue their children. The resulting inner array contains all nodes of one level. Right side view: the last node dequeued at each level is the rightmost visible node. Zigzag: alternate whether the level array is pushed left-to-right or right-to-left. Minimum depth: BFS finds the first leaf it encounters, which is guaranteed to be at the minimum depth. DFS might traverse deep branches before finding a shallower leaf.
lessons.analogy: BFS is like inspecting a building floor by floor. You fully inspect the ground floor before going to the first floor, and fully inspect the first floor before the second. The queue is your room list for the current floor: you add each room's sub-rooms to the list for the next floor. DFS is like following a single staircase all the way to the top, then coming back down and taking the next staircase. BFS finds the nearest floor with a fire exit; DFS might climb all the way to the top before finding one.

code_example.explanation: Zigzag uses index arithmetic (leftToRight ? i : levelSize-1-i) to place nodes at the correct position in a pre-sized array rather than pushing and reversing. This avoids an O(k) reverse call per level. The pre-sized array trick is a common pattern for level-based BFS problems.

common_mistakes: Not recording levelSize before the inner loop — as the inner loop runs, it enqueues children which grows the queue; if you check queue.length as the loop condition, you process children of the current level in the same loop as the current level
Using queue.shift() without noting it is O(n) — in interviews this is acceptable for clarity, but in production code use a proper head-pointer queue from Module 4 to keep each dequeue O(1)

Using DFS when BFS is explicitly required for level-order output — DFS with a level parameter can produce level-order results (DFS level order trick) but is harder to reason about; always use BFS for level-order problems
lessons.interview_relevance: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal (#102) is Blind 75. Binary Tree Right Side View (#199) and Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal (#103) are NeetCode 150. BFS is also the foundation of every shortest-path problem in graphs (Module 10). The level-grouping pattern (record levelSize before the inner loop) is used in all three of these problems and must be automatic.
lessons.mini_challenge: Implement levelOrder and verify it produces [[4],[2,7],[1,3,6,9]] for the example tree. Then implement Minimum Depth of Binary Tree (LeetCode #111): the minimum depth is the number of nodes along the shortest path from root to the nearest leaf. Use BFS and return the depth of the first leaf encountered. Explain why BFS is O(n) but better than DFS in practice for this problem when the tree is wide and the minimum depth is small.

flashcards.front: What data structure does BFS use?
flashcards.back: A Queue (FIFO). This guarantees all nodes at depth d are processed before any node at depth d+1.

flashcards.front: How do you group BFS results by level?
flashcards.back: Record queue.length (= levelSize) BEFORE the inner loop. Dequeue exactly that many nodes. Their children form the next level in the queue.

flashcards.front: Why is queue.shift() in JavaScript O(n)?
flashcards.back: Array shift() moves every element left by one position. For production, use a head-pointer queue or deque for O(1) dequeue.

flashcards.front: How do you get the Right Side View using BFS?
flashcards.back: In each level's inner loop, the LAST node dequeued (index === levelSize-1) is the rightmost visible node. Push it to result.

flashcards.front: Why is BFS better than DFS for minimum depth?
flashcards.back: BFS finds the FIRST leaf encountered, which is guaranteed to be at minimum depth. DFS may explore deep branches before finding a shallower leaf.

flashcards.front: What is the Zigzag trick in BFS?
flashcards.back: Use a pre-sized array and index arithmetic: idx = leftToRight ? i : levelSize-1-i. Avoids reversing each level separately.

flashcards.front: What does 'first time a node is visited' guarantee in BFS?
flashcards.back: It is the shortest path to that node. BFS processes nodes in increasing distance order from the source.

theory_mcq.question: Why is a QUEUE (FIFO) the correct data structure for BFS, while DFS uses a STACK (LIFO)?
options: Queue and stack are interchangeable for tree traversal

BFS must process all nodes at depth d BEFORE any node at depth d+1 — FIFO ordering guarantees this: nodes are dequeued in the exact order they were enqueued, so level-d nodes (enqueued first) are fully processed before any level-(d+1) nodes (enqueued during level-d processing) can be dequeued; a LIFO stack would process the LAST enqueued node next, immediately diving deep into one branch rather than finishing the current level
BFS only works with arrays, not queues or stacks
FIFO ordering is only needed when the tree has more than 2 levels
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson's explicit concept: 'Queue as the BFS data structure: FIFO ensures level-by-level' — this connects directly to Module 4's Queue lesson: FIFO processes items in arrival order, guaranteeing all same-level nodes are processed together before any deeper node is reached.

theory_mcq.question: In `levelOrder`, the variable `levelSize = queue.length` is captured AT THE START of each outer loop iteration. Why is this critical for correct level grouping?
options: levelSize is only used for loop bounds and doesn't affect grouping

At the start of each outer iteration, `queue.length` equals EXACTLY the number of nodes at the current level (all previously enqueued from the level above, none yet removed); by capturing this count in `levelSize`, the inner for-loop processes ONLY those level-d nodes, even though the queue GROWS during the loop as their children are enqueued for level d+1 — without capturing levelSize first, the loop would also process some d+1 nodes in the same iteration
levelSize is captured to avoid recomputing queue.length, which is O(n)
queue.length never changes during the inner loop
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the core trick for level-grouping: `queue.length` at the outer loop's start is exactly the count of level-d nodes waiting to be processed; as the inner loop dequeues them and enqueues their children, queue.length changes — capturing the initial count in `levelSize` gives the inner loop a FIXED boundary, ensuring it stops exactly when all level-d nodes are done, before processing any level-(d+1) children.

logic_mcq.question: For the reference tree (4/2,7/1,3,6,9), what does `levelOrder` return, what does `rightSideView` return, and what does `zigzagLevelOrder` return?
options: levelOrder=[[4],[2,7],[1,3,6,9]], rightSideView=[4,7,9], zigzagLevelOrder=[[4],[7,2],[1,3,6,9]] — all confirmed by direct execution
All three functions return [[4],[2,7],[1,3,6,9]]
logic_mcq.explanation: All confirmed by direct execution: levelOrder groups nodes by level into arrays-of-arrays; rightSideView takes the LAST node at each level (4 at level 0, 7 at level 1, 9 at level 2); zigzagLevelOrder reverses alternate levels (level 1 becomes [7,2] instead of [2,7], level 2 stays left-to-right producing [1,3,6,9]).

logic_mcq.question: In `zigzagLevelOrder`, how does `const idx = leftToRight ? i : levelSize - 1 - i;` achieve the alternating direction effect?
options: It reverses the entire level array after filling it

Instead of always pushing to the END of `level`, this pre-allocates `level` as a fixed-size array and places each node at a computed position: when `leftToRight=true`, node i goes to position i (left-to-right order); when `leftToRight=false`, node i goes to position `levelSize-1-i` (mirrored/reversed position) — the queue is always processed left-to-right, but nodes are PLACED at mirrored positions, achieving right-to-left output without reversing the queue
The formula reverses the queue order before processing
leftToRight only affects the root node's placement
logic_mcq.explanation: The key insight: the QUEUE always processes children in left-to-right order (BFS invariant), but by computing the placement index based on direction, nodes are written into the pre-sized `level` array at either their natural position (i) or its mirror (levelSize-1-i) — achieving the visual zigzag without any queue manipulation.

syntax_mcq.question: The lesson notes `queue.shift()` is O(n) and recommends a proper O(1) queue for large trees, but says it's 'acceptable for clarity' in interviews. Why is `shift()` O(n)?
options: shift() is O(1); the lesson's note is incorrect

Array `shift()` removes the FIRST element and must shift ALL remaining elements one position to the left to fill the gap, requiring O(n) work proportional to the array's current length — this is the exact same cost issue covered in Module 4 (Queues) where `arr.shift()` was identified as the naive, O(n) dequeue approach, and the head-pointer Queue class was introduced as the O(1) alternative
shift() is O(n) only when the array contains duplicate values
shift() is O(log n) when applied to sorted arrays
syntax_mcq.explanation: This directly references the Module 4 Queue lesson's core teaching: `shift()` is O(n) because removing from the front requires shifting all remaining elements — the same reason the efficient Queue class used a head-pointer instead; for interview clarity, the O(n) shift is acceptable on smaller inputs, but production BFS would use an O(1) dequeue implementation.

lessons.title: Height And Depth Of Trees
lessons.objective: Compute height and depth efficiently using recursive DFS, understand the O(n) lower bound for exact computation, and use height calculations as building blocks for diameter and balance problems.
concepts: Height recursion: height(node) = 1 + max(height(left), height(right))
Height of null: -1 (so leaf height = 0)
Maximum depth: same as height of root (LeetCode convention uses 1-indexed)
Minimum depth: BFS from Lesson 3 or careful DFS
O(n) time: every node visited exactly once
O(h) space: call stack depth equals tree height
Worst case O(n) space for skewed trees
Height as information passed upward: postorder pattern
lessons.explanation: Computing the height of a binary tree is the canonical postorder recursive pattern. The height of a node depends on the heights of its children, so children must be processed before the parent. The recurrence: height(null) = -1, height(node) = 1 + max(height(node.left), height(node.right)). Every node is visited exactly once: O(n) time. The call stack holds at most h frames where h is the tree height: O(h) space. For a balanced tree h = O(log n), so space is O(log n). For a skewed tree (essentially a linked list), h = n, so space is O(n). Maximum depth in LeetCode convention is 1-indexed (root has depth 1), which equals height(root) + 1 in the 0-indexed convention. Minimum depth requires care: a node with only one child is NOT a leaf, so its minimum depth is not 1 + the non-null child's depth. Minimum depth must find the nearest true leaf (both children null).
lessons.analogy: Height computation is like measuring the tallest person in a family tree by asking each family member how tall their tallest descendant is. Each person asks their children for the height of their tallest descendant, takes the maximum, adds 1 for themselves, and reports back to their parent. The root receives the answer for the entire tree. This bottom-up reporting is the postorder pattern.

code_example.explanation: The -2 sentinel in checkHeight allows early termination when an imbalance is detected deep in the tree. Without it, the function would compute heights for all nodes even after finding an imbalance, wasting work. This sentinel pattern (returning a special value to signal failure) is a common optimisation in tree problems that combine checking a condition with computing a value.

common_mistakes: Using minDepth without handling one-child nodes — a node with only a right child has minDepth = 1 + minDepth(right), not min(1 + 0, 1 + minDepth(right)); forgetting this produces incorrect answers for unbalanced trees

Confusing the LeetCode maxDepth convention (1-indexed, returns 1 for a single node) with the height convention (0-indexed, returns 0 for a leaf) — both are correct but mixing them in the same solution produces off-by-one errors

Not understanding that O(h) space for recursive height computation is O(n) in the worst case — a skewed tree (each node has only a right child) has height n-1, making the recursive call stack O(n) deep
lessons.interview_relevance: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree (#104) is Blind 75. Minimum Depth (#111) is NeetCode 150. Both are used as warm-up problems. Height computation is a subroutine in Balanced Binary Tree (#110) and Diameter of Binary Tree (#543). Being able to write maxDepth in 30 seconds from memory is the baseline, then explaining the one-child edge case in minDepth demonstrates attention to detail.

practice_problems.pattern: BFS or DFS with one-child guard

theory_mcq.question: Why does `minDepth` require special handling for nodes with only ONE child, compared to `maxDepth` which works correctly with just `Math.min(left, right)`?
options: minDepth and maxDepth have identical implementations; special handling is not needed

For a node with only a LEFT child (no right child), `minDepth(null) = 0` — naively taking `min(minDepth(left), 0) = 0` would incorrectly suggest the minimum path ends here (with no child), rather than continuing through the existing left child; the one-child guard says: if right child is absent, the only valid path goes through left (and vice versa) — a missing child is NOT a valid path endpoint, so its depth is excluded from the minimum
minDepth only needs special handling for the root node
minDepth and maxDepth differ only in whether they use min or max
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact explanation: 'Without the one-child guards: minDepth would return 1 + min(0, depth(right)) = 1 for a node with only right child, incorrectly treating the non-existent left path as depth 0' — a missing child is not a leaf (the definition requires BOTH children to be null), so its depth must not be considered as a valid minimum path.

theory_mcq.question: What does `checkHeight` returning -2 as a SENTINEL value accomplish, compared to returning the actual height?
options: Returning -2 signals the tree is empty

The -2 sentinel serves as an 'imbalanced' flag that propagates upward: once any subtree is found unbalanced (|leftH - rightH| > 1), -2 is returned INSTEAD of the actual height; parent calls check for this sentinel FIRST and immediately return -2 themselves without further computation — this enables EARLY TERMINATION, avoiding the O(n) remaining work that would be done if the check always returned actual heights and imbalance were detected only at the top
Returning -2 indicates the tree has exactly 2 levels
-2 is used to distinguish between left-heavy and right-heavy imbalances
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Sentinel value: return -1 (or -Infinity) to signal imbalance. Early termination: propagate sentinel upward without further work' — using a sentinel that's distinguishable from any valid height (all valid heights are >= -1) allows the check to short-circuit as soon as any imbalance is detected, making it O(n) rather than O(n) with full work for every subtree.

logic_mcq.question: What is the key difference between `maxDepth(root)` (LeetCode convention) and `height(root)` from Lesson 1, and how do the two relate mathematically?
options: They are identical; the same function with different names

Both measure the 'depth' of the tree but use DIFFERENT BASE CASES: `height(null) = -1` and `height(leaf) = 0` (edge-counting convention); `maxDepth(null) = 0` and `maxDepth(leaf) = 1` (node-counting convention, LeetCode standard) — they are related by `maxDepth(root) = height(root) + 1`: the same longest-path measured in EDGES (height) or in NODES (maxDepth)
height is always larger than maxDepth by exactly 2
maxDepth only works on perfect binary trees; height works on all trees
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit note: 'Maximum depth: same as height of root (LeetCode convention uses 1-indexed)' and 'maxDepth(null)=0, maxDepth(leaf)=1, maxDepth(root of 3-level tree)=3' — the relationship is `maxDepth(root) = height(root) + 1` because height counts edges (starting from 0 at leaves) while maxDepth counts nodes (starting from 1 at leaves).

logic_mcq.question: `nodeDepth` uses the pattern `left !== -1 ? left : nodeDepth(right, target, depth+1)` rather than computing both left AND right depth unconditionally. Why?
options: Both sides must always be searched; the ternary is just stylistic

This is short-circuit search: if `target` is found in the LEFT subtree (left !== -1 means left found it), there's no reason to search the right subtree at all — it returns the found depth immediately; only if left returns -1 (not found in left) does it search right; this avoids the O(n) cost of searching the entire tree when the target is in the left subtree, and mirrors the same optimization used in Module 6's `depthImpl` function
Searching right when left succeeds would return an incorrect result
The ternary is required because right depth is always -1
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the same short-circuit search pattern used in Module 6's linked list `depth` and Module 7 L1's `depthImpl`: once the left subtree confirms it found the target (returns a non-(-1) value), there's no need to explore the right subtree — early return avoids unnecessary work, though in the worst case (target in right subtree or absent) the full O(n) traversal still occurs.

syntax_mcq.question: In `minDepth`, why does the function check `!root.left && !root.right` BEFORE the one-child guards `!root.left` and `!root.right`?
options: The order of checks doesn't affect the result

The leaf check (`!root.left && !root.right`) must come first to correctly identify LEAF nodes (both children null) and return 1; if the one-child guards were checked first, the pattern `!root.left` would incorrectly match leaf nodes (which also have no left child) before the leaf case is identified, returning `1 + minDepth(root.right)` for what is actually a leaf — the top-to-bottom order of checks determines which case takes priority
Checking leaf first is purely a performance optimization with no correctness impact
The leaf check is never actually reached; the one-child guards handle all cases
syntax_mcq.explanation: If `!root.left` were checked before `!root.left && !root.right`, a leaf node (no left, no right) would match the `!root.left` guard (only-right-child case) and attempt `1 + minDepth(root.right)` — but `root.right` is also null for a leaf, giving `1 + minDepth(null) = 1 + 0 = 1`, which happens to be correct by coincidence but for the wrong structural reason; explicitly checking the leaf case first is clearer and avoids the subtle logic dependency.

lessons.title: Diameter Of A Binary Tree
lessons.objective: Compute the diameter of a binary tree in O(n) using a single postorder DFS pass, understanding why a naive two-pass approach is O(n²) and how sharing state via closure fixes it.
concepts: Diameter: longest path between any two nodes in the tree
Path may or may not pass through the root
Diameter through a node: leftHeight + rightHeight + 2 (counting edges)
Naive approach: compute diameter at every node separately — O(n²)
Single-pass O(n): compute height and update diameter simultaneously
Shared mutable state: closure or object to track global maximum
Edge vs node counting: diameter as edge count vs node count
Extension: longest path sum instead of longest count
lessons.explanation: The diameter of a binary tree is the length of the longest path between any two nodes. This path may or may not pass through the root. For any given node n, the longest path passing through n goes down its left subtree for leftHeight edges and down its right subtree for rightHeight edges. The diameter through node n = leftHeight + rightHeight + 2 (adding 2 for the two edges connecting node n to each subtree's deepest leaf). Wait — more precisely, if we define height as the number of edges to the deepest leaf, then diameter through n = height(left) + height(right) + 2. But LeetCode #543 counts edges so the answer for a single node is 0, not 2. The naive approach computes height(left) + height(right) at every node, but recomputes heights from scratch each time: O(n) per node, O(n²) total. The O(n) solution: during the single postorder height computation, track the maximum left+right sum seen at any node in a shared variable. The height function returns height while simultaneously updating the diameter maximum. This single-pass approach is the canonical example of combining two computations into one DFS.
lessons.analogy: Diameter is the widest point of a tree's canopy measured from one leaf-tip to another. For any junction (node), the widest path through that junction spans the deepest left branch plus the deepest right branch. The naive approach measures the canopy width at every junction by climbing down both sides from scratch each time. The O(n) approach measures both sides as part of a single root-to-leaf sweep, updating the maximum width seen at each junction along the way.

code_example.explanation: The closure variable maxDiameter is the shared state that accumulates the global maximum across all recursive calls. Each call to dfs returns the local height for the parent's use while also updating maxDiameter as a side effect. This pattern — returning one value while updating a shared maximum via closure — appears in dozens of tree problems including Balanced Binary Tree, Maximum Path Sum, and Longest Path.

common_mistakes: Computing height in a separate function call inside the diameter function — this produces O(n²) because height is recomputed from scratch at every node; combine both computations in a single DFS
Returning diameter instead of height from the dfs helper — the helper must return height (for the parent to use) not diameter; diameter is tracked separately in the closure variable

Off-by-one in diameter calculation — the diameter through a node with both children null (a leaf) should be 0 edges; verify: leftH=-1, rightH=-1, diameter=(-1+1)+(-1+1)=0; if you get 2, your formula needs adjustment
lessons.interview_relevance: Diameter of Binary Tree (#543) is Blind 75. The O(n) single-pass pattern it introduces — returning height while updating a global maximum via closure — is reused in Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum (#124, also Blind 75). Knowing how to combine two computations into one DFS pass is a high-signal technique that distinguishes candidates who have thought about tree optimisation.

flashcards.front: What is the diameter of a binary tree?
flashcards.back: The number of EDGES on the longest path between any two nodes. This path may or may not pass through the root.

flashcards.front: Formula for diameter through a node (edge count)?
flashcards.back: diameter_through_node = (leftHeight + 1) + (rightHeight + 1). Where leftHeight/rightHeight = height of left/right subtrees using null=-1 convention.

flashcards.front: Why is the naive diameter O(n²)?
flashcards.back: It calls height() separately at every node. height() is O(n) per call × n nodes = O(n²) total.

flashcards.front: How does the O(n) diameter solution work?
flashcards.back: Single postorder DFS. The helper returns height for the parent's use, while simultaneously updating a closure variable maxDiameter at each node.

flashcards.front: What closure variable pattern does diameter use?
flashcards.back: let maxDiameter = 0 outside dfs(). Inside dfs(), compute diameter = (leftH+1)+(rightH+1) and update maxDiameter = max(maxDiameter, diameter). Return height to parent.

flashcards.front: What does the dfs helper return in diameter — height or diameter?
flashcards.back: HEIGHT. The helper must return height so the parent can compute its own height and diameter. Diameter is tracked separately in the closure.

quiz.explanation: Calling height() at every node is O(n) per node × n nodes = O(n²). Combining both in one DFS is O(n).

quiz.explanation: diameter = (-1+1) + (-1+1) = 0. A single leaf has no edges for a path through it.

theory_mcq.question: Why is the naive `diameterNaive` O(n²) while `diameterOfBinaryTree` is O(n), even though both compute the same answer?
options: Both are O(n); the lesson's complexity claim is incorrect

diameterNaive calls `height()` AS A SEPARATE FUNCTION at every single node — since height itself is O(n), and this separate call happens at each of the n nodes, the total is O(n) × O(n) = O(n²); diameterOfBinaryTree computes height and updates the diameter SIMULTANEOUSLY in a single DFS pass, so height is computed once per node (not n times per node), giving O(n) total
The naive version is O(n²) only for unbalanced trees
diameterOfBinaryTree uses memoization to cache height values
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact explanation: 'height() called separately at every node -> O(n) per node -> O(n^2) total' for the naive version; the optimal version avoids this by doing both computations in one unified DFS — the same 'single-pass postorder' optimization pattern that appears in isBalanced (L6).

theory_mcq.question: In `diameterOfBinaryTree`, the inner `dfs` function updates `maxDiameter` via a CLOSURE rather than returning it. Why is this the appropriate mechanism here?
options: Closures are required by JavaScript for all nested functions

The `dfs` function must return the SUBTREE HEIGHT to its parent (for height computation), but also needs to update the GLOBAL maximum diameter — since a function can only have one return value, a shared variable via closure allows the two pieces of information (height returned up, diameter updated globally) to coexist without restructuring the return type or passing extra parameters down
Closures are faster than passing the maximum as a parameter
The diameter could alternatively be returned alongside the height with no trade-offs
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the core design trade-off: `dfs` returns the height (needed by the parent for its own diameter calculation), but also needs to maintain a running maximum — using a closure variable `maxDiameter` in the outer function's scope allows the inner `dfs` to update the global maximum at each node while still returning the height to satisfy the parent's computation needs.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `diameterOfBinaryTree` on the lesson's example tree (1 as root, 2 and 3 as children, 4 and 5 as children of 2). Per the lesson's trace, what diameter is recorded at node 2, and what is the final answer?
options: Diameter at node 2 is 1, final answer is 2

At node 2: leftH=0 (from dfs(4)) and rightH=0 (from dfs(5)), so diameter=(0+1)+(0+1)=2, maxDiameter updates to 2; at node 1: leftH=1 (from dfs(2)) and rightH=0 (from dfs(3)), so diameter=(1+1)+(0+1)=3, maxDiameter updates to 3; final answer is 3 — matching the lesson's exact trace and confirmed by direct execution
Both node 1 and node 2 record diameter 3
The diameter is computed only at the root, not at intermediate nodes
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace: 'dfs(2): L=0 R=0 diam=1+1=2. maxDiam=2. return 1. dfs(1): L=1 R=0 diam=2+1=3. maxDiam=3. return 2. Answer: 3' — the path 4→2→1→3 or 5→2→1→3 each span 3 edges, correctly identified at node 1.

logic_mcq.question: The diameter formula is `(leftH + 1) + (rightH + 1)`, where leftH and rightH are heights of subtrees (with null = -1). Why does `+1` appear for each side?
options: The +1 is a mistake; diameter should be leftH + rightH

leftH is the height of the left subtree (longest path DOWN from left child), and `leftH + 1` is the number of EDGES from the current node down to the deepest node in the left subtree — the +1 accounts for the edge from the current node to its left child; similarly for right; the total diameter through this node is the number of edges on both sides combined
+1 converts from node count to edge count globally
The formula is equivalent to leftH + rightH with different base cases
logic_mcq.explanation: With height(null) = -1 and height(leaf) = 0, the number of edges from a node to its deepest left descendant is `leftH + 1` (e.g., if left child is a leaf with height 0, there's 1 edge from current to the leaf = 0+1=1) — the total diameter through the current node is the sum of edges on both sides: (leftH+1) + (rightH+1).

syntax_mcq.question: In `diameterOfBinaryTree`, `maxDiameter` is declared with `let` in the OUTER function scope. What would happen if it were declared with `const` instead?
options: const works identically to let for this purpose

`const` prevents REASSIGNMENT of the variable — since `maxDiameter = Math.max(maxDiameter, diameter)` reassigns the variable at each node, using `const` would throw a TypeError at runtime; `let` is required here because the closure variable must be updated during the DFS traversal
const makes the variable private to the inner dfs function
Using const would make maxDiameter always equal to 0
syntax_mcq.explanation: `const` in JavaScript prevents reassignment (not mutation) — `maxDiameter = Math.max(...)` is a reassignment operation, which would throw a TypeError if maxDiameter were declared const; `let` is specifically the correct keyword for closure variables that need to be updated across multiple function calls.

lessons.title: Balanced Binary Tree Check
lessons.objective: Determine whether a binary tree is height-balanced in O(n) using a postorder DFS with early termination, avoiding the O(n²) naive approach.
concepts: Height-balanced definition: |height(left) - height(right)| <= 1 for every node
Naive O(n²): compute height separately at every node
Optimal O(n): combine height computation with balance check
Sentinel value: return -1 (or -Infinity) to signal imbalance
Early termination: propagate sentinel upward without further work
Bottom-up checking: imbalance at any node propagates immediately
Same single-pass pattern as diameter
AVL trees: balanced BSTs using this exact invariant
lessons.explanation: A height-balanced binary tree requires that for every node, the height difference between its left and right subtrees is at most 1. Naive check: call height(left) and height(right) separately at every node, check the difference. This is O(n) per node times O(n) nodes = O(n²). Optimal: combine the height computation with the balance check in a single postorder DFS. The helper function returns the actual height when the subtree is balanced, or a sentinel value (typically -1 in addition to the normal -1 for null, causing confusion — better to use a special value like -Infinity or throw an exception) when it is unbalanced. When a recursive call returns the sentinel, propagate it immediately without further computation. This early termination means work stops as soon as any imbalance is found. Each node is visited at most once: O(n). The clever implementation uses -2 or returns a {height, balanced} object.
lessons.analogy: Checking balance bottom-up is like a building safety inspector who checks structural integrity from the foundation up. If any floor is unsafe, the inspector immediately marks the whole building unsafe and stops inspecting floors above. The naive approach would have the inspector measure every floor independently, then compare. The optimal approach is a single sweep from bottom to top with immediate termination when a problem is found.

code_example.explanation: The -2 sentinel reuses -1 (which is the normal null height) and -2 (which can never be a real height) to encode two different states from a single return value. The cleaner object variant is more readable at the cost of object allocation per node. In interviews, the sentinel approach is more compact; in production code, the object variant is more maintainable.

common_mistakes: Using the naive O(n²) approach without realising it is suboptimal — in interviews, if you implement isBalancedNaive and do not mention the O(n²) issue, the interviewer will ask 'can you do better?'; always mention the O(n) optimisation

Choosing -1 as the unbalanced sentinel when height(null) is also -1 — this creates ambiguity; use a value that cannot be a valid height such as -2, -Infinity, or null, or use a two-field return object

Not short-circuiting after receiving the sentinel from a child — if you do not return the sentinel immediately after receiving it, the function continues computing heights for the rest of the subtree, negating the early termination benefit
lessons.interview_relevance: Balanced Binary Tree (#110) is Blind 75. It is a classic O(n²) vs O(n) discrimination problem. Candidates who give O(n²) without mentioning the improvement fail; candidates who immediately give O(n) with a clear sentinel explanation pass. The early-termination pattern using a sentinel value is also used in other tree problems including serialize/deserialize.

The optimal strategy: the middle element of the array becomes the root, then recurse on the left and right halves. This is LeetCode #108 Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree.

flashcards.back: For EVERY node in the tree, |height(left_subtree) - height(right_subtree)| ≤ 1. Must hold at every node, not just root.

flashcards.front: Why is the naive balanced check O(n²)?
flashcards.back: It calls maxDepth() separately at every node. maxDepth is O(n) per call, and there are n nodes = O(n²) total.

flashcards.front: How does the O(n) balanced check avoid O(n²)?
flashcards.back: Single postorder DFS that returns actual height when balanced, or a sentinel (-2) when unbalanced. Imbalance short-circuits without visiting remaining nodes.

flashcards.front: Why can't you use -1 as the unbalanced sentinel?

flashcards.front: What makes this problem the same pattern as diameter?
flashcards.back: Both combine two computations in one postorder DFS — returning one value (height) while checking/accumulating another (balance or diameter). Same template, different payloads.

flashcards.front: What is an AVL Tree?
flashcards.back: A self-balancing BST that maintains the height-balanced property (|leftH - rightH| ≤ 1) after every insert/delete via rotations. Guarantees O(log n) operations.

A tree is height-balanced if for EVERY node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by AT MOST 1 (|height(left) - height(right)| <= 1); requiring this at every node (not just the root) is essential because a tree could be balanced at the root but have deeply unbalanced subtrees deep inside — imbalance at any node can degrade BST operation performance from O(log n) to O(n)
Balanced means the tree has an even number of nodes
Balanced only requires the left and right subtrees to have the same height, not within 1

theory_mcq.question: What advantage does the 'cleaner variant' using `{ height, balanced }` return objects have over the sentinel (-2) approach, and what is its trade-off?
options: The object variant is always better in every way

The object variant is MORE READABLE: returning `{ height, balanced }` makes the meaning explicit — a reader immediately understands what each returned value represents without knowing the -2 sentinel convention; the trade-off is slightly MORE OVERHEAD (creating an object at every node vs returning a primitive integer) and LESS CONCISE code; the sentinel approach (-2) is more memory-efficient but requires knowing the sentinel convention to understand the code
The object variant doesn't support early termination; the sentinel does
Both approaches are identical in readability and performance
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson presents both explicitly: the sentinel approach returns either the actual height or -2 as a special flag (compact but requires knowing the convention), while the object approach returns explicit fields (more self-documenting but slightly heavier due to object allocation per node) — both achieve O(n) time with early termination.

Imbalance is detected at node 4 (the leaf)
Every node independently returns -2 regardless of subtree height

dfs(9)=0 (leaf), dfs(15)=0 (leaf), dfs(7)=0 (leaf), dfs(20): leftH=0, rightH=0, |0-0|=0 ≤ 1, returns 1; dfs(3): leftH=0 (node 9), rightH=1 (subtree 20/(15,7)), |0-1|=1 ≤ 1, returns 2; all nodes satisfy |leftH-rightH| ≤ 1, so isBalanced returns true — confirmed by direct execution

Node 3's children have heights 2 and 0, failing the check

syntax_mcq.question: In `isBalancedClean`, why does the early-exit branch return `{ height: 0, balanced: false }` rather than `{ height: -1, balanced: false }` or some other height value?
options: The height value in the early-exit is critical and must be exactly 0

When returning an 'unbalanced' sentinel object, the `height` field's value doesn't actually matter for correctness — the parent will check `left.balanced` (or `right.balanced`) first and short-circuit before ever using the height value; returning `height: 0` is a reasonable placeholder, but returning any integer would work equally well since the height is never consumed when balanced=false

lessons.title: Maximum Depth And Path Sum
lessons.objective: Solve Maximum Depth, Path Sum, and Path Sum II using DFS, understanding how path information is passed downward through the recursion and collected on return.
concepts: Maximum depth: maxDepth from Lesson 4, Blind 75 baseline
Path Sum I: does any root-to-leaf path sum to target?
Top-down DFS: pass remaining target down, return true/false
Path Sum II: collect all root-to-leaf paths summing to target
Backtracking in tree DFS: add node on entry, remove on exit
Path Sum III: count paths summing to target, not just root-to-leaf
Prefix sum technique on paths: reuse Module 3 prefix sum pattern
Maximum path sum: any path (Lesson 5 extension)
lessons.explanation: Path problems on trees use DFS with a parameter that carries state downward. Path Sum I: pass a remaining target down the recursion. At each node, subtract the node's value from the remaining target. At a leaf, check if the remaining target equals 0. This is a top-down DFS where information flows from root to leaf. Path Sum II requires collecting all valid paths. Use backtracking: maintain a current path array. On entry to a node, push the node's value. On exit (after both recursive calls), pop it. At each leaf where the sum matches, copy the current path to the results. The pop on exit is the backtracking step that restores the path state for sibling branches. Path Sum III (any path summing to target, not just root-to-leaf) uses prefix sums: maintain a hash map of prefix sum to count, exactly like the Subarray Sum Equals K pattern from Module 3, applied vertically along a root-to-node path.
lessons.analogy: Top-down path DFS is like a hiker counting their remaining food budget as they walk down a mountain path. They start with a full budget at the root and subtract the cost of each segment as they go. At the bottom (leaf), they check if they have spent exactly their budget. Backtracking in Path Sum II is the hiker erasing their path notes when they retrace to try a different fork, so the notes are always accurate for the current path.

code_example.explanation: In pathSumIII, the backtracking step prefixCounts.set(currentSum, count-1) is critical. Without it, a prefix sum from one root-to-node path would incorrectly influence a sibling path. The map must only contain prefix sums from the current active path, not from previously visited paths. This is the same invariant maintained in the 2D prefix sum for Subarray Sum Equals K.

common_mistakes: Not making a copy of the path when adding to results in pathSum II — result.push(path) pushes a reference; as path is modified by later backtracking, all results will point to the same empty array at the end; always push [...path] or path.slice()
Forgetting to backtrack (pop) after recursive calls in pathSum II — without the pop, the path keeps growing and never represents the current root-to-node path correctly

Not reverting the prefixCounts map entry in pathSumIII after returning from a node — prefix sums from one branch must not pollute the sibling branch; the decrement after both recursive calls is mandatory
lessons.interview_relevance: Maximum Depth (#104) and Path Sum (#112) are Blind 75. Path Sum II (#113) and Path Sum III (#437) are NeetCode 150. The backtracking pattern introduced in Path Sum II is the direct prerequisite for the Backtracking module (L2-M04). Understanding how to maintain and restore path state in tree DFS is essential for every tree-based backtracking problem.

flashcards.front: How does Path Sum I work?
flashcards.back: Top-down DFS. Pass remaining = targetSum - node.val downward. At a LEAF, return remaining === 0. At null, return false.

flashcards.front: What backtracking means in Path Sum II?
flashcards.back: push node.val when entering, pop after both recursive calls exit. This restores the path to its state before this node for sibling branches.

flashcards.front: Critical error in Path Sum II: result.push(path)?
flashcards.back: This pushes a REFERENCE. As backtracking modifies path, all results become the same empty array. Always push [...path] or path.slice() to copy.

flashcards.front: How does Path Sum III extend Path Sum I?
flashcards.back: Paths can start AND end at any node, not just root-to-leaf. Uses prefix sum hash map on the current path — same pattern as Subarray Sum Equals K.

flashcards.front: Why must Path Sum III backtrack the prefixCounts map?
flashcards.back: Prefix sums from one branch must NOT influence sibling branches. Decrement the count after visiting both children to restore the map for sibling DFS calls.

flashcards.front: Information flow direction in path problems?
flashcards.back: Top-down: pass remaining target DOWN via parameters (Path Sum I, II). Bottom-up: return gain UP via return value (Max Path Sum). Both combined = powerful.

theory_mcq.question: In `hasPathSum`, why is the leaf check `!root.left && !root.right` paired with `root.val === targetSum` rather than `root.val === 0` or some other condition?
options: The condition should check root.val === 0 since targetSum is always decremented to 0 at leaves

Each recursive call passes `targetSum - root.val` (the REMAINING sum after accounting for the current node) — at a leaf, the leaf's own value hasn't yet been subtracted; so the correct check is whether the leaf's value EQUALS the remaining target (i.e., `root.val === targetSum`, meaning this node exactly accounts for the last needed amount); if targetSum were tracked as a running 'used' total rather than 'remaining', the check would differ
Checking root.val === targetSum only works at the root, not at leaves
The condition doesn't matter at leaves since they always return true
theory_mcq.explanation: The function passes the REMAINING target downward: `hasPathSum(root.left, targetSum - root.val)` — at each recursive call, the current node's value is subtracted from the remaining target BEFORE passing it down; but note the subtraction happens in the RECURSIVE CALL, not before the leaf check — so at the leaf, targetSum still holds the value expected INCLUDING this leaf's contribution, hence `root.val === targetSum`.

theory_mcq.question: In `pathSum` (Path Sum II), why does `path.pop()` execute AFTER the recursive calls, and what would happen if it were omitted?
options: path.pop() has no effect on the algorithm's correctness

`path.pop()` is the BACKTRACKING step — it removes the current node from the path before returning to the parent, restoring the path to its state before entering this node; without pop(), every node visited would PERMANENTLY accumulate in `path`, so when the DFS explores different branches, nodes from completed branches would remain in `path`, contaminating subsequent path constructions with incorrect values from already-completed branches
path.pop() is only needed when a match is found, not at every node
Omitting pop() would cause the function to crash due to array overflow
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit concept: 'Backtracking in tree DFS: add node on entry, remove on exit' — this is the standard tree DFS backtracking pattern: `path.push(node.val)` on entry + DFS recursive calls + `path.pop()` on exit ensures the path array always reflects only the nodes on the CURRENT root-to-node path, correctly shared across all branches.

logic_mcq.question: In `pathSumIII` (Path Sum III), what does `prefixCounts.get(currentSum - targetSum) || 0` compute, and why does the prefix sum Map start with `Map([[0, 1]])`?
options: It counts nodes with value equal to targetSum; the initial 0 is a placeholder

At any node, `currentSum - targetSum` is the prefix sum that would need to have occurred EARLIER in the path for a subpath ending HERE to sum to targetSum; looking up how many times that prefix sum has been seen gives the count of valid subpaths ending at this node; the initial `Map([[0, 1]])` handles subpaths starting from the ROOT: a prefix sum of 0 (empty prefix) occurs once, so if currentSum equals targetSum exactly, the lookup `prefixCounts.get(0)` finds 1, correctly counting the root-to-current path
The initial Map entry prevents null pointer errors in the lookup
prefixCounts only tracks the path from the root; subpaths not starting at the root are not counted
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's comment: '// sum 0 seen once (empty path)' — this is the same prefix sum technique from Module 3 (Hashing): to count subarray sums equal to target, we ask 'how many earlier prefix sums equal currentSum - target?' (those sums would have been subtracted to give a range sum of target); initializing 0→1 correctly handles the full path from root to current node.

logic_mcq.question: Why must `pathSumIII` DECREMENT `prefixCounts` for `currentSum` in the backtracking step (after recursive calls), rather than simply clearing the entire map?
options: Clearing the map would be more efficient and correct

When DFS backtracks from the current node (moving back up to the parent), this node's prefix sum contribution must be REMOVED from the map — but the MAP stores prefix sums for ALL ancestors currently on the active path; decrementing only the current node's entry correctly removes this node's contribution while PRESERVING all ancestor prefix sums still in use by sibling branches; clearing the entire map would destroy ancestor prefix sums needed for other paths
Decrementing is needed only for nodes where a path sum match was found
The map is never modified during backtracking; the backtrack step is a no-op
logic_mcq.explanation: The prefix sum map represents the set of prefix sums along the CURRENT root-to-node path — when DFS moves from the current node back to its parent (backtrack), the current node leaves the active path and its prefix sum contribution must be removed; a full clear would destroy the parent and grandparent prefix sums still valid for subsequent sibling branch explorations.

syntax_mcq.question: In `pathSum`, `result.push([...path])` uses spread `[...path]` rather than `result.push(path)`. Why is copying the array necessary?
options: Both are equivalent; spread is just stylistic

Pushing `path` directly would push a REFERENCE to the same shared array object — since `path` is mutated by backtracking (pop operations), all previously-pushed references would see the SAME final (empty) array after the DFS completes; spreading `[...path]` creates a SHALLOW COPY of the current path values at this moment, capturing the path's current state as an independent array that won't be affected by subsequent push/pop operations
Spread is required because path is a generator, not a real array
Copying prevents the path from being pushed to result multiple times
syntax_mcq.explanation: This is the standard 'snapshot the path' pattern for backtracking: pushing the array reference would make all stored paths point to the same mutable object, which would be empty after DFS completes; `[...path]` creates an independent copy at the moment of the match, preserving the path values permanently in `result` even as the original `path` continues to be modified by subsequent DFS steps.

lessons.title: Binary Search Tree — Insert And Search
lessons.objective: Implement BST insert and search using the BST invariant, understand why O(h) operations become O(n) on unbalanced trees, and know when BSTs are preferable to hash maps.
concepts: BST invariant: left subtree values < node value < right subtree values
Strict vs non-strict inequality: handling duplicates
Search: O(h) by going left or right based on comparison
Insert: search for the correct leaf position, attach new node
Delete: three cases — leaf, one child, two children
In-order successor: used in two-child deletion
O(h) operations: O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed
BST vs hash map: BST maintains sorted order, supports range queries
lessons.explanation: A Binary Search Tree is a binary tree with a critical invariant: for every node, all values in its left subtree are strictly less than the node's value, and all values in its right subtree are strictly greater. This invariant enables O(h) search where h is the tree height: at each node, compare the target to the current value. If equal, found. If less, the target must be in the left subtree. If greater, in the right subtree. This halves the search space at every step (for a balanced tree). Insert follows the same path as search, stopping when a null child is reached and inserting there. Delete has three cases: (1) Leaf: just remove. (2) One child: replace node with its child. (3) Two children: replace the node's value with its in-order successor (the smallest value in the right subtree), then delete the in-order successor from the right subtree. The in-order successor is always either a leaf or has only a right child (it has no left child by definition of being the leftmost node in the right subtree).
lessons.analogy: BST search is like finding a word in a physical dictionary. At each page, you check: is my word earlier or later than what's on this page? You skip half the remaining dictionary with each check. An unbalanced BST where all values are inserted in sorted order degenerates to a linked list — like a dictionary where every word is on a different page in a single stack you must flip through one by one.

code_example.explanation: deleteNode returns the modified root at every recursive level. When the target is found and deleted, the function returns its replacement (right child, left child, or the modified subtree with the successor deleted). The caller assigns the return value back: root.left = deleteNode(root.left, key) correctly updates the parent's pointer. This return-and-reassign pattern is the cleanest way to modify tree structure in recursive functions.

common_mistakes: Not returning root at the end of insertIntoBST — without returning root, the parent cannot link the new node into the tree; the recursive insert pattern requires returning root at every level so the parent can do root.left = insertIntoBST(root.left, val)

Not handling the two-child deletion correctly — copying the in-order successor's value and then deleting the successor from the right subtree is the clean approach; do not swap the nodes themselves as this complicates pointer management

Assuming BST operations are always O(log n) — for an unbalanced BST (e.g. inserting [1,2,3,4,5] in order), the tree degenerates to a right-skewed linked list with O(n) operations; self-balancing BSTs (AVL, Red-Black) maintain O(log n) but are not typically implemented in interviews
lessons.interview_relevance: Search in a Binary Search Tree (#700) and Insert into a BST (#701) are standard warm-ups. Delete Node in a BST (#450) is NeetCode 150. The in-order successor concept appears in BST Iterator (#173, Blind 75). Knowing that inorder traversal of a BST produces sorted output unlocks Kth Smallest Element in BST (#230, Blind 75) immediately: do inorder traversal and return the kth element.

Implement kthSmallest(root, k): return the kth smallest value in a BST in O(h+k) time. Use inorder traversal with an early exit when k reaches 0. Then implement BST Iterator (LeetCode #173): a class with next() returning the next smallest value and hasNext() returning whether more values exist. Use an explicit stack to simulate inorder iteration.

flashcards.front: State the BST invariant precisely.
flashcards.back: For every node N: ALL values in N's left subtree < N.val < ALL values in N's right subtree. Must hold for the entire subtree, not just direct children.

flashcards.front: BST search: which way do you go?
flashcards.back: If target < node.val → go LEFT. If target > node.val → go RIGHT. If target === node.val → found. If node is null → not found.

flashcards.front: BST insert: why must you return root?
flashcards.back: The recursive call does root.left = insertIntoBST(root.left, val). Without returning root at every level, the parent cannot link the new node. Missing return = lost node.

flashcards.front: BST delete: 3 cases?

flashcards.front: What is the in-order successor in BST delete?
flashcards.back: The smallest value in the right subtree — go right once, then left as far as possible. It has no left child, so deleting it is case 1 or 2.

flashcards.front: When is BST better than a hash map?
flashcards.back: When you need: sorted order, in-order iteration, range queries (all values between a and b), find next larger/smaller, or floor/ceiling operations. Hash maps don't support these.

flashcards.front: BST worst case: when does it become O(n)?
flashcards.back: When elements are inserted in sorted order (e.g. 1,2,3,4,5). The tree becomes a right-skewed linked list with height n-1 and O(n) operations.

theory_mcq.question: What is the BST invariant, and how does it enable O(h) search rather than O(n)?
options: The BST invariant requires all nodes to have exactly 2 children

The BST invariant states: all values in a node's LEFT subtree are LESS THAN the node's value, and all values in the RIGHT subtree are GREATER THAN the node's value (strict inequality) — this means at each step during search, a single comparison (`val < root.val` or `val > root.val`) eliminates one entire subtree from consideration; since roughly HALF the remaining tree is discarded at each level (in a balanced tree), the search takes O(h) steps = O(log n) for a balanced BST
The BST invariant only applies to leaf nodes
BST invariant means all values are stored in sorted order in an array
theory_mcq.explanation: The BST invariant (left < parent < right, applied recursively to ALL descendants, not just immediate children) is what enables the binary decision at each node — 'go left' or 'go right' — discarding the other subtree entirely, giving O(h) search. For a balanced BST, h = O(log n); for a skewed tree, h = O(n).

theory_mcq.question: In BST deletion, why is the THREE-CHILD case (node has both left and right children) the most complex, and what role does the IN-ORDER SUCCESSOR play?
options: The two-child case is no more complex than the one-child case

When a node with TWO children is deleted, simply removing it would leave two disconnected subtrees with no clear reattachment point; the in-order successor (the smallest node in the RIGHT subtree, found by going right once then all the way left) is the node that would COME NEXT in sorted order — replacing the deleted node's VALUE with the successor's value, then deleting the (simpler, at most one-child) successor node from the right subtree, cleanly maintains the BST invariant
The two-child case always requires rebuilding the entire tree
The in-order successor is the largest node in the left subtree
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's algorithm: 'Case 3: two children — find in-order successor (min of right subtree)... replace value... delete successor' — the in-order successor is the minimum of the right subtree (go right once, then leftmost), which is always larger than everything in the left subtree and smaller than everything else in the right subtree, making it the correct replacement that preserves the BST invariant.

logic_mcq.question: After inserting [5,3,7,1,4,6,8] into an empty BST using `insertIntoBST`, what does `inorder(bstRoot)` return, and why?
options: [5,3,7,1,4,6,8] — values in insertion order

[1,3,4,5,6,7,8] — inorder traversal of a BST always produces sorted ascending output, as confirmed by direct execution; the BST invariant guarantees the inorder visit order (left→root→right) matches ascending value order
[8,7,6,5,4,3,1] — inorder produces descending order
[5,3,1,4,7,6,8] — inorder follows insertion order for BSTs
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: `console.log(inorder(bstRoot)); // [1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]` — the BST invariant guarantees inorder traversal produces a sorted sequence regardless of insertion order, since inorder visits left (all smaller) then root then right (all larger) at every node.

logic_mcq.question: In `insertIntoBST`, why does the function `return root` at the end of the recursive case (when the node exists), rather than just modifying the child pointer and returning nothing?
options: return root is unnecessary; the function could return void

The recursive style works by REASSIGNING child pointers at each level: `root.left = insertIntoBST(root.left, val)` — the left/right assignment at the parent level receives the return value of the recursive call (which may be an existing node OR a newly-created node at the base case) and sets it as the child; `return root` (for existing nodes) and `return new TreeNode(val)` (base case) both participate in this pointer-return chain; without returning root for existing nodes, the parent would set its child pointer to undefined, severing the subtree
return root speeds up the algorithm by avoiding null checks
BST insertions always replace the root; the return value selects the new root
logic_mcq.explanation: The 'return and reassign' pattern is the standard recursive tree modification approach: at each level, `root.left = insertIntoBST(root.left, val)` uses the RETURN VALUE to set the child pointer; when the current node isn't the insertion point, `return root` passes the unchanged current node back up so the parent correctly re-links its child; the base case `return new TreeNode(val)` provides the actual new node to link.

syntax_mcq.question: In `deleteNode`, when the target node is found and has BOTH children, why does the code `root.val = successor.val` followed by `root.right = deleteNode(root.right, successor.val)` rather than physically moving the successor node?
options: It's impossible to move a node in a BST; only values can be changed

Physically moving a node (relinking its predecessor's next pointer) in a tree would require knowing the successor's parent — tracking the parent requires extra state or a separate traversal; COPYING the successor's value into the current node and then DELETING the (simpler) successor from the right subtree achieves the same semantic result (node 'removed' from the BST) with only O(h) additional work for the successor deletion, using the same deleteNode function recursively
Moving nodes would violate the BST invariant; only value copying is safe
root.val = successor.val only works when the successor is the root's direct right child
syntax_mcq.explanation: The value-copy approach elegantly reuses the existing recursive `deleteNode` for the successor removal: instead of complex pointer relinking (which would require parent tracking), the trick overwrites the target's value with the successor's value (maintaining BST invariant since successor is the minimum of the right subtree), then recursively deletes the successor from the right subtree using the same function.
