lessons.title: BST Validation
lessons.objective: Validate whether a binary tree satisfies the BST invariant using min/max bounds propagation, and understand why checking only parent-child relationships is wrong.
concepts: BST invariant: all values in left subtree < root < all values in right subtree
Why checking only immediate children is wrong
Min/max bounds approach: pass valid range down the recursion
Left subtree: max bound tightens to parent value
Right subtree: min bound tightens to parent value
Base case: null node is always valid
Integer overflow with Integer.MIN/MAX in Java/C++ (not JS)
Inorder traversal approach: must produce strictly increasing sequence
lessons.explanation: Validating a BST is more subtle than checking that each node's left child is smaller and right child is larger. Consider: root=5, left subtree root=4, left subtree's right child=6. Checking only parent-child pairs: 4<5 (ok), 6>4 (ok). But 6>5 violates the BST invariant — it is in the left subtree of 5 but greater than 5. The correct approach propagates valid bounds down the recursion. Every node must satisfy: min_bound < node.val < max_bound. Initially min_bound=-Infinity and max_bound=+Infinity. When we go left, we tighten the max_bound to the current node's value. When we go right, we tighten the min_bound to the current node's value. Any node that violates its bounds makes the tree invalid. Alternative approach: inorder traversal must produce a strictly increasing sequence for a valid BST. Track the previous inorder value and fail if the current value is not strictly greater.
lessons.analogy: BST validation with bounds is like a game of Password where each node must stay within the rules set by all its ancestors, not just its parent. Going left means 'all your descendants must be less than me' — a constraint that applies to the entire left subtree, not just the immediate left child. The naive check (only parent-child) is like checking that each person knows only their direct supervisor's password, missing that there is a company-wide rule they also must satisfy.

code_example.explanation: The bounds approach propagates two constraints down the tree: every node must be greater than its leftmost ancestor that it is to the right of, and less than its rightmost ancestor that it is to the left of. The inorder approach is cleaner to reason about (BST inorder = sorted) but requires a closure variable. Both are O(n) time and O(h) space. In interviews, either is acceptable; stating both and choosing one demonstrates thoroughness.

common_mistakes: Only checking immediate parent-child relationships — this is the most common BST validation mistake; always validate against the full range constraints accumulated from all ancestors

Using <= instead of < for the min bound check (or >= instead of >) — BST requires strictly greater and strictly less; equal values should make the tree invalid (per standard BST definition); check node.val > min and node.val < max strictly

Using Integer.MIN_VALUE as the initial min bound in Java or C++ — if the tree contains Integer.MIN_VALUE, the bound check fails incorrectly; use null as the initial bound and handle it with a conditional, or use -Infinity (which works in JavaScript and Python)

flashcards.back: A node's left subtree can contain a value that is less than the node but GREATER than the node's parent. This violates the BST invariant but passes the parent-child check.

flashcards.front: BST validation: bounds approach?
flashcards.back: Every node must satisfy min_bound < node.val < max_bound. Going left: max tightens to current node's val. Going right: min tightens to current node's val. Initially (-∞, +∞).

flashcards.front: BST validation: inorder approach?
flashcards.back: Inorder traversal of a valid BST produces strictly increasing values. Track prev value. If current.val ≤ prev → invalid.

flashcards.back: Strictly < and >. BST requires no duplicates (standard definition). node.val must be STRICTLY greater than min_bound and STRICTLY less than max_bound.

theory_mcq.question: Why is checking only IMMEDIATE children (`root.left.val < root.val` and `root.right.val > root.val`) WRONG for BST validation?
options: Checking immediate children is correct and sufficient

The BST invariant requires all values in the left subtree (not just the direct left child) to be less than the current node — a deeply nested descendant could violate the global constraint even if all parent-child pairs locally satisfy the invariant; the lesson's counterexample illustrates this: a tree rooted at 5 with right child 6 having a left child 3 passes the parent-child check (3>parent 6's parent check fails... wait — actually 3 passes its local check against parent 6 since 3<6) but 3 is in the RIGHT subtree of 5, so 3<5 violates the BST property globally
The issue only arises when the tree has more than 3 levels
Checking immediate children is correct; the lesson contains an error
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact counterexample: tree [5, 4, 6, null, null, 3, 7] — node 3 has parent 6 (3<6 passes local check) but 3 is in the RIGHT subtree of 5, so 3<5 is a global BST violation; `isValidBSTWrong` returns true for this tree (confirmed by execution), demonstrating that local parent-child checks are insufficient.

theory_mcq.question: How does the min/max bounds approach in `isValidBST` correctly propagate the GLOBAL BST constraint at every node?
options: It propagates the constraint by checking every pair of nodes

At each node, valid values must lie in the range (min, max); going LEFT tightens the UPPER bound (the current node's value becomes the new max — nothing in the left subtree can exceed the current node); going RIGHT tightens the LOWER bound (the current node's value becomes the new min — nothing in the right subtree can be below the current node); this recursively passes down the full ancestral constraint, not just the immediate parent's constraint
min/max bounds are only valid for the root's direct children
The approach uses a sorted array to verify the constraint
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `isValidBST(root.left, min, root.val)` (left: upper bound tightens to root.val) and `isValidBST(root.right, root.val, max)` (right: lower bound tightens to root.val) — each recursive call carries the accumulated constraints from ALL ancestors, not just the immediate parent, correctly enforcing the global BST invariant.

logic_mcq.question: Verify `isValidBST` on the invalid tree [5, 4, 6, null, null, 3, 7] from the lesson. At which node is the violation detected, and what bounds does it violate?
options: The violation is detected at node 6 (the right child of 5)

The violation is detected at node 3: when isValidBST recurses to node 3 (the left child of 6), the bounds are (min=5, max=6) — inherited from the path 5→right→6→left; checking node 3: 3 <= min=5 is TRUE (3 ≤ 5), so the condition `root.val <= min` fires and returns false; confirmed by direct execution showing isValidBST(invalidBST) === false
The violation is detected at the root (node 5)
isValidBST correctly returns true for this tree; the wrong function is the one that fails
logic_mcq.explanation: Tracing: isValidBST(5, -∞, ∞) → isValidBST(6, 5, ∞) → isValidBST(3, 5, 6): at node 3, `3 <= 5` (root.val <= min) is true → returns false; confirmed by execution and the lesson's console.log: `isValidBST(invalidBST) // false`.

logic_mcq.question: How does `isValidBSTInorder` (the inorder approach) detect BST violations, and what does it track to do so?
options: It collects all values into an array and checks if it's sorted afterward

It maintains a `prev` variable initialized to -Infinity, updated to the current node's value after each inorder visit; if any node's value is NOT strictly greater than `prev` (i.e., `node.val <= prev`), the BST property is violated (the sequence would not be strictly ascending); by failing immediately on first non-increasing value, it achieves O(n) time with early termination, processing the inorder sequence on-the-fly without storing all values
It compares each node to its parent's value directly
The inorder approach is less efficient than the bounds approach and is only a backup
logic_mcq.explanation: The inorder approach exploits the equivalence: a valid BST ↔ its inorder traversal is STRICTLY increasing; tracking only the previous value (prev) and checking `node.val <= prev` at each step gives O(n) time O(h) space validation without storing the full inorder sequence, failing fast at the first violation.

syntax_mcq.question: In `isValidBST`, the bounds start as `min = -Infinity, max = Infinity`. Why does JavaScript's `Infinity` work correctly here, while some languages (Java, C++) require `Integer.MIN_VALUE` / `Integer.MAX_VALUE` and risk overflow?
options: Infinity in JavaScript is the same as Integer.MAX_VALUE in Java

JavaScript uses 64-bit floating-point numbers (IEEE 754 doubles) which natively represent positive and negative Infinity as actual values that compare correctly with any finite number — `any_number > -Infinity` and `any_number < Infinity` are always true; Java and C++ integer types have FIXED maximum/minimum values that could be valid BST node values themselves (e.g., Integer.MIN_VALUE could appear as an actual node value), creating incorrect bounds comparisons, which the lesson notes with 'Integer overflow with Integer.MIN/MAX in Java/C++ (not JS)'
JavaScript's Infinity only works for trees with at most 100 nodes
Both languages use Infinity; the lesson note is incorrect
syntax_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit note: 'Integer overflow with Integer.MIN/MAX in Java/C++ (not JS)' — JavaScript's native `Infinity` and `-Infinity` are IEEE 754 special values that genuinely represent unbounded bounds, safely usable as initial min/max; languages with fixed-width integers must use Long.MIN/MAX_VALUE or separate null-checks to avoid treating the sentinel as a valid node value.

lessons.title: Tree Problem Thinking
lessons.objective: Given any tree problem, select DFS or BFS, identify the traversal order, and know whether information flows top-down or bottom-up within 60 seconds of reading the problem.
concepts: DFS vs BFS decision: depth/path problems vs level/shortest-path problems
Traversal order decision: preorder (top-down), inorder (BST sorted), postorder (bottom-up)
Information flow: top-down (pass state down), bottom-up (return state up)
Combining top-down and bottom-up in the same DFS
Module 7 Blind 75 / NeetCode 150 problems mapped to patterns
BST problems: always use the BST invariant, not generic tree approach
Skills unlocked: Binary Trees, BST, DFS, BFS
Bridge to Module 8: Tries use the same tree node structure
lessons.explanation: Tree problems decompose into four decisions. First: DFS or BFS? DFS for depth, path, height, diameter, subtree-level questions. BFS for level-order, minimum depth, or shortest-path questions. Second: which DFS order? Preorder when the answer at a node depends on what was seen on the path from the root (top-down: pass depth, path sum, bounds). Inorder when you need the BST sorted property. Postorder when the answer at a node depends on values from its subtrees (bottom-up: height, diameter, balance, subtree count). Third: how does information flow? Top-down: pass parameters through recursive calls going into the tree. Bottom-up: return values back up from recursive calls. Fourth: is it a BST? If yes, use the BST invariant to eliminate half the tree at every step; do not use generic tree traversal. Combining top-down and bottom-up in one DFS is the most powerful pattern: pass depth or path sum downward while returning height or subtree answers upward.
lessons.analogy: Tree problem thinking is like choosing the right tool for an inspection job. BFS is the floor-by-floor inspector: use it when you need to report by level. DFS preorder is the top-down investigator: use it when the result at a node depends on what was found above. DFS postorder is the bottom-up analyst: use it when the result depends on what was found below. BST is a specialised tool: when the tree has the sorting property, exploit it instead of treating the tree generically.

Using a generic tree approach (visiting all nodes) for BST problems instead of exploiting the BST invariant to prune half the tree — this makes O(log n) problems O(n)

flashcards.back: When the problem is about LEVELS: level order output, right side view, zigzag, minimum depth, or 'nearest' in terms of depth.

flashcards.front: When do you choose DFS preorder?
flashcards.back: When information flows TOP-DOWN from root to leaf: path from root, remaining budget, depth passed as parameter, bounds for BST validation.

flashcards.front: When do you choose DFS inorder?
flashcards.back: When you need the BST SORTED property: kth smallest, BST validation (inorder approach), serializing sorted BST output.

flashcards.front: When do you choose DFS postorder?
flashcards.back: When information flows BOTTOM-UP: height, diameter, balance check, subtree count, any answer at a node that depends on its children's answers.

flashcards.front: What is the BST short-circuit principle?
flashcards.back: For BST problems, use the BST invariant to PRUNE half the search space at each node. Going left/right based on comparison turns O(n) generic traversal into O(h) = O(log n) balanced.

BFS: 'level order', 'right side view', 'zigzag', 'minimum depth', 'by level'; DFS Preorder: 'path from root to leaf', 'depth of node', 'paths summing to target'; DFS Inorder: 'kth smallest', 'validate BST', 'sorted output'; DFS Postorder: 'height', 'diameter', 'balanced', 'subtree count', 'invert tree'
All tree problems use DFS postorder; BFS is only for graphs
BST problems always use BFS; general tree problems always use DFS
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact decision tree: BFS for level/breadth problems; DFS preorder for top-down path problems; DFS inorder for BST sorted-property problems; DFS postorder for bottom-up aggregation problems where child information is needed before parent processing.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson specifically note 'BST problems: always use the BST invariant, not generic tree approach'?
options: Generic tree approaches never work on BSTs

BSTs have the ADDITIONAL structural property (left < parent < right, recursively) that GENERIC tree algorithms don't exploit — a problem like 'search for a value' on a generic tree requires O(n) traversal, but on a BST the invariant enables O(h) search by eliminating one subtree at each step; likewise, BST validation, kth smallest, and LCA all have O(h) or O(log n + k) solutions specific to BSTs that are faster than the O(n) solutions that would be required for a generic tree
BST problems require a completely different programming language
Generic tree approaches are always correct on BSTs; they're just slower
theory_mcq.explanation: The BST invariant is additional structural information that unlocks more efficient algorithms — problems that require O(n) traversal on generic binary trees can often be solved in O(h) = O(log n) on BSTs by leveraging the sorted property; the lesson's decision tree explicitly flags this to prevent students from defaulting to generic O(n) DFS/BFS when O(h) BST-specific approaches exist.

logic_mcq.question: A problem says 'find the height of each node and return nodes where height > 3'. Applying the lesson's decision tree, which traversal order is required, and why?
options: BFS, because we need to process all nodes at each level

DFS POSTORDER — the signal is 'height', which the lesson explicitly maps to DFS postorder ('height, diameter, balanced, subtree count'); height is a BOTTOM-UP measure (computed from children up to parent), requiring children's heights to be known BEFORE the parent can compute its own height; preorder would process the parent before children, making height unavailable; inorder would interleave parent and child processing incorrectly
DFS Preorder, because we process nodes from root downward
Any traversal works equally well for this problem
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact decision tree: 'USE DFS POSTORDER when: height, diameter, balanced, subtree count, invert tree' — height is paradigmatically bottom-up: a node's height = 1 + max(left_height, right_height), which requires both children's heights to be computed FIRST (postorder processes children before parent).

logic_mcq.question: Per the lesson's Module 7 problem map, how many problems are Blind75, and which traversal pattern covers the MOST Blind75 problems?
options: 5 Blind75 problems; BFS covers the most

11 problems are Blind75 (confirmed by direct execution: all except #112 Path Sum); DFS postorder covers the most: Maximum Depth (#104), Diameter (#543), Balanced Tree (#110), and Invert Binary Tree (#226) — at least 4 of the 11 Blind75 problems in this module use postorder bottom-up processing
All 12 problems are Blind75
7 Blind75 problems; DFS inorder covers the most
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: `module7_problems.filter(p => p.blind75).length` returns 11 (all except #112 Path Sum with blind75:false); scanning the 11 Blind75 entries, DFS postorder appears for at least Maximum Depth, Diameter, Balanced Tree, and Invert Binary Tree — the 'bottom-up height/subtree-info' pattern is the most common paradigm in this module's Blind75 set.

syntax_mcq.question: In `module7_problems`, a problem like 'LCA of Binary Search Tree' (#235) has `pattern: 'BST path split'` rather than a generic DFS descriptor. What does 'BST path split' signal about the algorithm strategy?
options: BST path split means the tree is physically split into two separate trees

For LCA (Lowest Common Ancestor) on a BST, the algorithm exploits the BST invariant to determine which subtree contains each target node: if both targets are less than the current node, recurse left; if both are greater, recurse right; if they split (one less, one greater, or one equals current), the current node IS the LCA — no general DFS scan needed; 'path split' refers to the moment the two target nodes' paths diverge, which can be identified in O(h) using only comparisons
Path split means the path from root to target is stored in a split array
BST path split is identical to the bounds-propagation approach in BST validation
syntax_mcq.explanation: The BST LCA algorithm works by walking the path and finding where the two target values 'split' — one goes left, one goes right (or one matches the current node) — this is the O(h) BST-specific approach vs. the O(n) generic tree LCA that must handle arbitrary structures.
